The next obvious question would be how did the blastocyst develop from a fertilized egg and now the answers become less assured. At that time, we had and still have two hypothetical answers: the so-called inside–outside hypothesis (Tarkowski & Wróblewska, 1967) and the polarization hypothesis (Johnson & Ziomek, 1981). The inside–outside hypothesis basically stated that following the fourth division of the newly formed embryo (from the 8- to 16-cell stage), some blastomeres are located inside while others are outside.

The community of mammalian developmental biologists passionately discussed this issue, and though we all believed that mouse development is in principle regulative, most of us had some reservations about the strength of the experimental evidence. It would require too much space to go into detail here, so one example of the controversy will have to suffice (for more details, see Gardner, 1996). A single mouse blastomere from a 2-cell stage embryo can develop into an entire animal and a single blastomere from either 4- or 8-cell stage embryos can participate in all embryonic and extraembryonic tissues in chimeras, suggesting their identity and totipotency (Kelly, 1975, 1977).

These experiments weigh against developmentally relevant cytoplasmic localizations in the zygote and indicate that all components necessary for development are equally distributed throughout the egg. However, one could argue (since not every blastomere from a 2-cell stage embryo develops into a mouse nor every blastomere from 4- and 8-cell stage embryos participates in every tissue in a chimera) that there is cytoplasmic localization of essential components in all zygotes and when these components are allocated to one blastomere of the 2-cell stage embryo, this one will develop into an adult and its sister blastomere will not.

In terms of timing, studies in mouse embryos suggest that the onset of compaction could be controlled by the decrease in the nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio that takes place during the early cleavage divisions and/or the dilution of a potential inhibitor of compaction present in the zygote (Kojima et al., 2014).

Human embryos in which compaction is either initiated prematurely or delayed have a lower potential to form blastocysts (see Glossary, Box 1). Premature compaction is associated with cytokinetic failure and multi-nuclear blastomeres (Iwata et al., 2014), whereas delayed compaction is associated with a reduced number of inner cell mass (ICM) cells (see Glossary, Box 1) (Ivec et al., 2011).
